samples.text:
Protecting the environment is one of the biggest challenge in the world today. Some people say that big companies are mainly responsible for this, not the normal consumers. I agree with this statement to a large extent, but I also think individuals have some responsibility.

The main reason why I agree is that large companies cause most of the pollution. Factories produce a lot of smoke and waste, and many companies use huge amount of plastic for packaging their products. One company can make more pollution in one day than thousands of people in one year. Also, companies have a lot of money and technology, so they are able to change their production to more green methods, for example using solar energy or recycled materials. If the big companies change, the effect on the environment will be very big.

In addition, consumers often do not have a choice. When a person goes to supermarket, almost every product is wrapped in plastic, so even if he want to avoid plastic, it is very difficult. That is why the companies should take the first step and give people environmental friendly products with reasonable price.

However, individuals are also important. Companies make products because consumers buy them. If people buy less things and choose products from companies that care about nature, the companies will be forced to change. Also, people can save electricity at home and use bus instead of car.

In conclusion, I believe that the large companies has the main responsibility for protecting the environment because they create the most pollution and they have the power to change. However, consumers should also do their part by making better choices in daily life.

samples.text:
There is ongoing debate about who should carry the main burden of protecting the environment. Some people believe that large corporations bear the greatest responsibility, while ordinary consumers play only a minor role. I largely agree with this view, although I think consumers have an important part to play in pushing companies to change.

The most convincing reason for placing responsibility on large companies is the scale of their impact. Energy firms, manufacturers and major retailers are responsible for a large share of carbon emissions, waste and deforestation, often far more than any individual could produce in a lifetime. A single decision by a multinational to switch to renewable energy or reduce packaging can therefore have a greater effect than millions of individual efforts. Companies also possess the financial resources and technical expertise needed to develop cleaner processes, which most households simply do not have.

Furthermore, consumers' choices are shaped and limited by what companies offer. It is difficult for someone to live sustainably if affordable products are all packaged in plastic or if public transport is poorly developed. In this sense, blaming individuals can distract attention from the structural changes that are really needed, and some businesses may even encourage this focus to avoid stricter regulation.

Nevertheless, consumers are not powerless. Businesses respond to demand, so when large numbers of people buy second-hand clothes or avoid products linked to environmental damage, companies have a strong incentive to adapt. Individual behaviour, such as reducing food waste or flying less, also add up when it is widespread and can help to create social pressure for government action.

In conclusion, I agree that large companies should take the main responsibility for protecting the environment because of their enormous impact and resources. However, consumers still have a meaningful role, mainly by using their purchasing power to hold those companies accountable.

samples.text:
Whether environmental protection is chiefly the duty of large corporations or of individual consumers is a question that shapes how societies respond to climate change and pollution. In my view, the primary responsibility does lie with major companies, but framing the issue as a choice between the two risks overlooking how closely their behaviour is connected.

The case for holding corporations principally accountable is persuasive. Industrial production, energy generation and global supply chains account for a large share of emissions, and decisions taken in a handful of boardrooms determine how goods are made, transported and packaged for millions of people. When a major retailer eliminates single-use plastics or an airline invests in cleaner fuels, the environmental gain dwarfs anything a conscientious shopper could achieve alone. Companies also have the capital to fund research into cleaner technologies, and they are the ones that profit from environmentally harmful practices, which strengthens the moral argument for making them pay for the damage.

Moreover, emphasising personal responsibility can be misleading. Consumers can only choose from the options available to them, and sustainable alternatives are often more expensive or simply unavailable. A family living in a suburb without reliable public transport, for instance, has little choice but to drive. Urging such people to change their habits while leaving corporate practices largely untouched shifts the burden onto those with the least power to solve the problem.

This is not to say that individuals are irrelevant. Collective consumer behaviour sends signals that companies cannot ignore, and public pressure is often what persuades governments to regulate industry more strictly. The growth of demand for plant-based food and electric vehicles illustrates how shifting preferences can reshape entire markets.

Overall, I agree that large companies bear the greater responsibility, given their scale, resources and profits. Consumers, however, remain an important catalyst, since their choices and political pressure help to ensure that corporations actually meet that responsibility.
